text: We know containers share the host's kernel instead of booting their own. So what stops one container from seeing another's files, or starving it of CPU? Two Linux kernel features: namespaces and cgroups. Docker didn't invent either one -- it packages them into an easy-to-use tool.

A namespace gives a process its own isolated view of one kind of system resource. Docker combines several: a PID namespace so a container only sees its own processes, a network namespace for its own IPs and ports, a mount namespace for its own view of the filesystem, and a user namespace so a container's "root" can map to an unprivileged user on the host.

Here's what that looks like in practice. Run an Ubuntu container interactively and list its processes, and you'll only ever see that container's own processes starting from PID 1 -- never anything else running on the host. That's the PID namespace doing its job.

Namespaces control what a container can see. Control groups, or cgroups, control what it can use -- limiting and accounting for CPU, memory, disk, and network. Docker sets sensible defaults automatically, and you can override them per container, like capping this one at half a CPU core and 512 megabytes of memory.

Put those two together and you've got the technical definition of a container: one or more processes running with namespaces applied for isolation and cgroup limits applied for resource control. At Northbridge, that's what keeps a bug in the catalog service from touching checkout's files, and what keeps a traffic spike in one from starving CPU the other one needs.
Next, in Lesson Four, we'll get Docker actually installed and running on your machine.
